Pool boiling experiment characteristics on the pure copper surface
Xiaoli Huang1, Zeliang Chen1 (), Nan Gui1, Xingtuan Yang1, Jiyuan Tu1,2, Shengyao Jiang1 ()
1. Institute of Nuclear and New Energy Technology, Collaborative Innovation Center of Advanced Nuclear Energy Technology, Key Laboratory
of Advanced Reactor Engineering and Safety, Ministry of Education, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China
2. School of Engineering, RMIT University, Melbourne, VIC 3083, Australia
Abstract
The pool boiling characteristics with different boiling surfaces and working fluids play an
important part in multiphase flow research. The key parameters of pool boiling, such as heat
transfer coefficient (HTC) and critical heat flux (CHF), can be only acquired by experiment. Thus, a
pool boiling experimental device is designed and produces the HTC and CHF data on the pure
copper heating surface, which are 72.25 kW/(m2.K) and 1093.28 kW/m2, respectively. Besides, a
series of visualization experimental results of bubble behavior in the pool boiling are taken by the
high-speed camera to provide references for the boiling mechanism research. The pool boiling
experiment would be the benchmark data to validate the future experiments and computer
simulations.

pool boiling
critical heat flux (CHF)
heat transfer coefficient (HTC)

1 Introduction
Boiling heat transfer is one of the most effective phase
change heat transfer methods. It can utilize the huge
latent heat of vaporization of the boiling liquid to transfer
or dissipate high heat flux with a minimal temperature
difference between the heat transfer surface and the liquid
(Vakarelski et al., 2012; Cho et al., 2015, 2017). Thus, it plays
an important part in heat energy transfer and conversion
of industries, such as electricity generation, refrigeration
equipment, electronics cooling, etc. The enhancement in
boiling performance can bring immediate benefits to
improve the efficiency, safety, and cost in energy systems,
leading to energy savings and greenhouse gas emission
reduction.
The two most important parameters in boiling heat
transfer are boiling heat transfer coefficient (HTC) and
critical heat flux (CHF) (Wang and Chen, 2018), which
respectively characterized the heat transfer efficiency and the
allowable heat transfer capacity. The CHF, a phenomenon
also known as the boiling crisis (Lloveras et al., 2012), occurs
accompanied by the sharp deterioration on the rate of
HTC from boiling surface to coolant (Yang et al., 2021),
and leads to the sudden shift of flow regime from nucleate
boiling to film boiling, which results in drastic increasing
of surface temperature with disastrous consequences, for
example, the degradation of surface material, the destruction
of device components, and the thermal meltdown of the
systems (Rahman et al., 2015; Jaikumar et al., 2017).
As the most basic one in the boiling experiments, the
pool boiling experiment could be a feasible idea to get the
key parameters of the boiling heat transfer and provide
references for boiling mechanism research (Berenson, 1962;
Dhillon et al., 2015). Besides, the pool boiling experiment
would be the benchmark data for the computer simulations
and other boiling experiments (McVay et al., 2015).
In this study, we get the HTC and CHF data on the
pure copper surface from the pool boiling experimental
device. In addition, the photos of bubbles at different heat
flux have been captured by the high-speed camera.
2 Pool boiling experimental device

heating component, auxiliary heater, data acquisition device,

2.1 Boiling pool chamber and heating component
The overall dimensions of the boiling pool chamber are
160 mm × 120 mm × 150 mm. The wall of the chamber was
made of 3 mm thick glass, while the bottom and top were
respectively made of thermal insulated Teflon plate and
FR4 fiberglass board. The boiling pool chamber was directly
open to the atmosphere by the hole on the top plate, in order
to keep the pool boiling experiment under atmospheric
pressure.
Copper is one of the most widely used materials in
scientific studies and engineering applications because
of its excellent good processing properties and physical
performance, such as high thermal conductivity and high
electrical conductivity. As a result, copper is used as a base
material in the current study. As shown in Fig. 1(b), the
heating component consisted of a copper component and
eight heating rods (Φ12 mm × 90 mm), which connected to
the DC power supply (MAISHENG MP25020D DC power
supply) with max power 5 kW (250 V, 20 A). The upper
part of the copper component was a cylinder with 20 mm
in diameter and 36 mm in height, while the bottom part
was a cuboid with 90 mm in length, 65 mm in width,
and 35 mm in height. The heating rods with max power
250 W were inserted into the bottom part of the copper
component and directly provided heat flux to the heating
component.
The upper part of the heating component passed
through a hole located at the center of the Teflon bottom
plate. A high-temperature silicone gasket was used to seal
the gap between the heating component and the boiling
pool chamber, in order to avoid the working fluid leakage
of the experimental device and prevent boiling from
occurring at the edge of the copper heating surface. Besides,
the whole heating component was wrapped in the
high-temperature resistance thermal insulated fiberglass

After solving the liquid leakage and heat loss, the distilled
water, as working fluid, was heated and maintained at
saturation temperature (Tsat) by a K-type thermocouple
and the auxiliary heater (250 V, 250 W) placed inside the
boiling pool chamber.

were 1 mm, marked by T1, T2, and T3) were installed inside

100-200 °C, which is about 389-393 W/(m.K), is large

cylinder can consider as one-dimension heat conduction.

3 Pool boiling experiment on the pure copper surface
3.1 Experimental method
Before the experiment, the pure copper surface of the
heating component was polished by 2000 mesh sandpaper
and cleaned with 95% ethyl alcohol. Subsequently, the
heating component was assembled inside the pool boiling
experimental device and the formal experiment began.
The main steps of a formal pool boiling experiment are as
follows:
Step 1: The distilled water in the boiling pool chamber was
heated by the auxiliary heater and maintained at saturation
temperature (1 atm, 100 °C) for over 30 min, in order to
eliminate the non-condensable gas in the working fluid.
Step 2: The heating component was switched on and kept
at a steady-state condition, which is applied to calculate
the heat flux and the boiling heat transfer performance.
Each of the steady-state conditions was characterized by
the maximum temperature fluctuations of T1, T2, and T3
no more than 0.5 °C/min. The final steady-state data
were the average of the temperature data collected by the
data acquisition device (A-BF BCL2008S Multichannel
temperature recorder) in 1 min. During the steady-state
condition, photos should be taken by the high-speed camera
to analyze the bubble behavior of the pool boiling.
Step 3: The heat flux supplied to the pure copper heating
surface was stepwise increased by turning up the DC
power supply, until the critical heat flux (CHF) occurred,
whose phenomenon is not only the sharp increment of
thermocouples temperature but also the film boiling on the
heating surface.
Step 4: When the CHF phenomenon had occurred, the
power source should be decreased or shut down before the
heating component temperature is too high to break down
the thermocouples or heating rods.

When the CHF phenomenon is approached, the boiling
surface is covered by a vapor film formed by vigorous
coalescence between lots of bubbles on the heating surface,
leading to a transition from nucleate boiling regime to film
boiling regime. As a result, heat transfer between the heating
surface and the working fluid is blocked by the vapor film,
causing heat transfer deterioration which will characterize
as sudden and dramatic wall temperature increment
(Fig. 2(a)).
Figure 2(b) shows the comparison of the pool boiling in
this work and other studies (Kwark et al., 2010; Wu et al.,
2010; Lai, 2017). The obtained steady-state condition and
CHF data are similar with both the experimental and
theoretical results of pure surfaces in the other studies,
verifying the accuracy and reliability of the current
experimental device and method.
The same as the empirical trend, the HTC increases
with the increase of heat flux, as shown in Fig. 2(c), but the

rate of increment somewhat decreases at the high heat flux.
The HTC reaches the peak when the CHF phenomenon
occurs.
All of the steady-state condition data are shown in
Table 2 and the corresponding visualization experimental
results are shown in Fig. 3. From visual inspection through
high-speed CCD, at the beginning of the experiment, the
bubbles are small and independent (Fig. 3(a)). With the
rising of the heat flux, the small bubbles gather together
and grow larger on the copper surface (Figs. 3(b) and 3(c)).
The larger the heat flux rose, the growth and enlargement
of localized hot/dry regions are easier to form large vapor
slugs (Figs. 3(d) and 3(e)). The vapor slugs and bubbles will
vigorously coalesce even further when the heat flux keeps
increasing, until the formation of a vapor blanket that
covers the boiling surface, which means a boiling regime
transition (Fig. 3(f)).
4 Conclusions
In this work, the recent saturated pool boiling experimental
results were introduced, which were conducted at atmospheric pressure using the pure copper as heating surface
and the distilled water as working fluid. The HTC is
72.25 kW/(m2.K) and the CHF is 1093.28 kW/m2, which were
obtained by the specially designed pool boiling experimental
device. Furthermore, the visualization experimental results
of pool boiling, such as typical nucleate boiling and typical
film boiling, have been captured by the high-speed camera
in order to provide references for future boiling mechanism
research.
The experimental results have shown the skillfully
master of pool boiling experimental technology. In future
work, the proposed approach is easily scalable to various
material surfaces or different working fluids, for example,
the graphene coating surface or nanofluid. The pool boiling
experiment would be the benchmark data in the future
experiments. Furthermore, the computer simulations would
be validated by the experimental results.
In conclusion, it is believed that the boiling experiment
in the current work is of great importance for the
enhancement of efficiency and safety in the energy industry,
particularly demonstrating the feasibility of developing a
high-performance and durable heat exchange surface.
